newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-BHP cleans slate, eyes asset sales.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BHP cleans slate, eyes asset sales.

text.p: Australia's largest listed company, The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP), on Friday reported a plunge in net annual profit and wiped clean its balance sheet.

The steel, mining and petroleum group announced a 60.8 percent fall in earnings after abnormal items to just A$410 million for the year ended May 31, after slicing over A$800 million from the book value of its global asset base.
But the write-downs, including A$550 million at its North American copper assets, masked an improvement in underlying pre-abnormal earnings, which rose seven percent.
The share market warmed to the result, especially BHP's move to fix its balance sheet, and sent BHP shares nine cents higher on the day to close at A$19.15.
"They have certainly wiped the slate clean," a Melbourne analyst told Reuters.
BHP swallowed almost A$1 billion in net abnormal losses for the year, including A$220 million for restructuring its steel division and major write-downs of minerals and petroleum assets.
"I am confident we are laying the foundation for a better result going foward," BHP managing director John Prescott told a news conference.

They began revising their BHP profit forecasts for 1997/98 closer to A$2 billion before abnormals, thanks to a much lower depreciation charge on the trimmed-down asset base and signs of upturn in the company's copper and steel businesses.
Before the profit announcement, analysts were expecting BHP to report net earnings of around A$1.9 billion in 1997/98.
Prescott said no more abnormal asset write-downs would be made in 1997/98.
But question marks still remained over some of BHP's assets, including some of the North America copper mines bought only 18 months ago when BHP paid US$2.4 billion for the Magma Copper Co.
Prescott glaringly omitted the Magma assets in outlining BHP's "key, core assets" on Friday.
BHP is the world's second largest producer of copper.
Prescott listed BHP's core assets as the low-cost Escondida copper mine in Chile, oil and gas fields in Australian waters, parts of its steel division and its iron ore and coal business.
The rest he classed as second-league assets which could be considered for sale to the highest bidder.
